$comment: What causes disease, what it does, how bad it is, and what answers it. NOT a recipe: recipes are the game's two-input grammar and say how a thing is derived. This is the unbounded honest answer about an organism, the way needs.json is the unbounded honest answer to 'what goes into one'. Two rules it exists to enforce. First, seriousness is a SOURCED NUMBER and never an adjective, because 'serious' would rank the catalogue by how frightening a thing sounded when it was written up; the same organism has several true numbers — untreated and treated, bubonic and pneumonic — so the basis is stated with the value. Second, nothing here is a method: the game explains how these things work and never how to obtain, culture or spread them, which is the line cautions.json draws too. `wanted` drives authoring the same way a needs list does. See tools/pathogens.mjs.

rabies_virus.transmission: the saliva of a biting mammal
rabies_virus.reservoir: bats, and dogs where dogs are not vaccinated
rabies_virus.makeup: single negative-strand RNA, about 12 kb, in a bullet-shaped envelope
rabies_virus.durability: minutes outside a host — it does not survive drying

seriousness.measure: case fatality once symptoms begin; fewer than twenty survivors are recorded

hiv.transmission: blood, sex, and mother to child
hiv.reservoir: humans; it entered from primates in the early 20th century
hiv.makeup: two copies of single positive-strand RNA, 9.7 kb, with reverse transcriptase carried inside the capsid
hiv.durability: does not survive outside the body in any practical sense

seriousness.measure: untreated, progression to AIDS and death is near-universal; median about eleven years

measles_virus.transmission: air, and it is among the most transmissible things known — R0 of 12 to 18
measles_virus.makeup: single negative-strand RNA, about 16 kb, enveloped
measles_virus.durability: up to two hours in the air of a room after the infected person has left

seriousness.measure: case fatality in well-nourished populations; ten to fifty times that where malnutrition is common

poliovirus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA, 7.5 kb, in a bare protein capsid with no envelope
poliovirus.durability: weeks in water and sewage — the bare capsid is why

seriousness.measure: paralytic cases; about one infection in two hundred becomes paralytic at all

influenza_virus.reservoir: wild waterfowl, and pigs, which is where the reassortment happens
influenza_virus.makeup: eight separate segments of negative-strand RNA — the segmentation is what lets two strains swap whole genes
influenza_virus.durability: hours on hard surfaces, longer in cold dry air

seriousness.measure: seasonal influenza, symptomatic case fatality; the 1918 strain was about 0.025

yellow_fever.reservoir: monkeys, in a forest cycle the human one spills out of
yellow_fever.makeup: single positive-strand RNA, about 11 kb, enveloped — a flavivirus
yellow_fever.durability: needs the mosquito; it does not persist in the environment

seriousness.measure: the toxic phase, which about one case in seven reaches

west_nile_virus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA flavivirus, about 11 kb, enveloped

seriousness.measure: neuroinvasive cases; under one per cent of infections become neuroinvasive at all

norovirus.transmission: faecal-oral, and vomit aerosols — as few as eighteen particles will do it
norovirus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA, 7.5 kb, bare capsid
norovirus.durability: weeks on surfaces, and it survives most alcohol hand gels

seriousness.measure: case fatality, almost all of it in the very old

rhinovirus.transmission: hands and surfaces more than air
rhinovirus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA picornavirus, bare capsid; over 160 serotypes, which is why immunity never accumulates

seriousness.measure: not a cause of death in healthy hosts

adenovirus.makeup: double-stranded DNA, 36 kb, bare icosahedral capsid with fibres at the vertices
adenovirus.durability: weeks on surfaces, and resistant to lipid disinfectants because it has no envelope

seriousness.measure: negligible in healthy hosts; serious in the immunosuppressed

cytomegalovirus.transmission: saliva, urine, and across the placenta
cytomegalovirus.reservoir: humans; most adults carry it for life
cytomegalovirus.makeup: double-stranded DNA, 235 kb — one of the largest genomes of any human virus
cytomegalovirus.durability: latent in the host's own cells indefinitely
symptoms: retinitis and colitis where immunity is absent

seriousness.measure: immunocompetent hosts; the harm falls on transplant patients and the unborn

human_papillomavirus.makeup: double-stranded circular DNA, 8 kb, bare capsid
human_papillomavirus.durability: persists in the epithelium for years

seriousness.measure: acute infection; the harm is cervical cancer decades later, and types 16 and 18 cause most of it

rubella.makeup: single positive-strand RNA togavirus, 10 kb, enveloped

seriousness.measure: the disease itself is trivial; caught in the first trimester it deafens or blinds the child

mumps.makeup: single negative-strand RNA paramyxovirus, 15 kb, enveloped

seriousness.measure: case fatality; the common harm is deafness and, after puberty, sterility

hepatitis_a.transmission: faecal-oral, usually through food or water
hepatitis_a.makeup: single positive-strand RNA picornavirus, bare capsid
hepatitis_a.durability: months in water; it survives drying and mild heat

seriousness.measure: case fatality, rising sharply over fifty

cowpox.reservoir: voles and wood mice, despite the name
cowpox.makeup: double-stranded DNA poxvirus, about 224 kb, brick-shaped and enveloped
cowpox.durability: very durable — poxvirus particles survive years in dried scab material

seriousness.measure: a local lesion in a healthy host; its importance is that surviving it protects against smallpox

tobacco_mosaic_virus.transmission: contact — hands, tools, and the plants rubbing together
tobacco_mosaic_virus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA, 6.4 kb, in a rigid rod of 2,130 identical protein subunits
tobacco_mosaic_virus.durability: decades in dried leaf, and it survives boiling — which is why it was the first virus ever isolated

seriousness.measure: it rarely kills the plant; the loss is in yield and leaf quality

yersinia_pestis.transmission: the bite of a flea that has fed on an infected rodent
yersinia_pestis.makeup: Gram-negative rod, 4.65 Mb, with three plasmids the harmless soil ancestor did not have
yersinia_pestis.durability: days in a flea, longer in a cool burrow

seriousness.measure: untreated bubonic plague; the pneumonic form untreated approaches 1.0

bacillus_anthracis.transmission: contact with infected animals or their hides and wool
bacillus_anthracis.reservoir: grazing animals, and soil, where the spore waits
bacillus_anthracis.makeup: Gram-positive rod, 5.2 Mb, with a protein capsule and two toxin plasmids
bacillus_anthracis.durability: spores remain viable in soil for decades, which is the whole epidemiology

seriousness.measure: untreated inhalational anthrax; the cutaneous form untreated is about 0.2

mycobacterium_tuberculosis.transmission: air, from someone with an open lung cavity
mycobacterium_tuberculosis.reservoir: humans, a quarter of whom carry it latently
mycobacterium_tuberculosis.makeup: a rod with a waxy mycolic-acid wall that takes neither Gram stain properly; 4.4 Mb
mycobacterium_tuberculosis.durability: months in dried sputum away from sunlight

seriousness.measure: untreated pulmonary tuberculosis, over about ten years

clostridium_tetani.transmission: a wound that closes over dirt
clostridium_tetani.makeup: Gram-positive anaerobic rod that makes a terminal spore, giving it a drumstick shape

seriousness.measure: untreated generalised tetanus

clostridium_botulinum.transmission: food preserved without enough salt, acid or heat
clostridium_botulinum.makeup: Gram-positive anaerobic rod; its toxin is the most acutely poisonous protein known
clostridium_botulinum.durability: spores survive boiling — only pressure canning reaches them

seriousness.measure: treated foodborne botulism; before antitoxin it was about 0.6

corynebacterium_diphtheriae.makeup: Gram-positive club-shaped rod; the toxin gene is carried in by a bacteriophage, so untouched strains are harmless
corynebacterium_diphtheriae.durability: weeks in dust and on fomites
symptoms: a grey membrane across the throat

seriousness.measure: untreated respiratory diphtheria

bordetella_pertussis.transmission: droplets, and it is highly transmissible

seriousness.measure: infants under one year, untreated

treponema_pallidum.transmission: sexual contact, and across the placenta
treponema_pallidum.makeup: a spirochaete so thin it cannot be seen by ordinary light microscopy; 1.1 Mb, one of the smallest of any free-living bacterium
treponema_pallidum.durability: dies within hours outside the body — it cannot even be grown routinely in culture
symptoms: a rash on palms and soles

seriousness.measure: untreated, over several decades

salmonella.transmission: food and water contaminated with faeces
salmonella.reservoir: poultry, reptiles, and human carriers for typhoid
salmonella.makeup: Gram-negative rod with peritrichous flagella, about 4.8 Mb
salmonella.durability: weeks in water, months in dried faeces, and it survives freezing

seriousness.measure: untreated typhoid fever

e_coli.transmission: food and water, and it is normally a harmless gut resident
e_coli.reservoir: the intestine of every warm-blooded animal
e_coli.makeup: Gram-negative rod, 4.6 Mb; the dangerous strains carry a Shiga toxin brought in by a phage
e_coli.durability: days to weeks in water and on produce

seriousness.measure: haemolytic uraemic syndrome following Shiga-toxin strains

listeria_monocytogenes.transmission: chilled ready-to-eat food — soft cheese, pâté, smoked fish
listeria_monocytogenes.makeup: Gram-positive rod that moves inside host cells by polymerising their own actin behind it
listeria_monocytogenes.durability: it grows at refrigerator temperature, which is what makes it a food-safety problem at all

seriousness.measure: invasive listeriosis

legionella.transmission: aerosols from cooling towers, showers and spa pools — never person to person
legionella.makeup: Gram-negative rod that survives inside amoebae, which is the training that lets it survive inside human macrophages
legionella.durability: indefinitely in a biofilm at 25 to 45 degrees

seriousness.measure: treated Legionnaires' disease

staphylococcus_aureus.reservoir: the nose of about a third of healthy people
staphylococcus_aureus.makeup: Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters, 2.8 Mb; the resistant strains carry an extra penicillin-binding protein
staphylococcus_aureus.durability: months on dry surfaces, and it tolerates salt and drying better than most

seriousness.measure: bacteraemia

streptococcus_pyogenes.makeup: Gram-positive cocci in chains, 1.9 Mb, with an M protein that resists being eaten by white cells
symptoms: and rarely a rapidly spreading soft-tissue infection

seriousness.measure: invasive group A streptococcal disease

streptococcus_pneumoniae.reservoir: the human nose and throat, carried harmlessly by many children
streptococcus_pneumoniae.makeup: Gram-positive diplococci with a polysaccharide capsule; the capsule is the vaccine target and there are over ninety types of it

seriousness.measure: pneumococcal pneumonia, treated

helicobacter_pylori.transmission: probably faecal-oral in childhood, within families
helicobacter_pylori.reservoir: the human stomach, in about half of all people
helicobacter_pylori.makeup: a curved rod with a sheathed flagellum; it makes urease to raise the pH immediately around itself
helicobacter_pylori.durability: it lives in stomach acid, which nothing else does

seriousness.measure: the ulcer itself; the long tail is gastric cancer, and it is the only bacterium classed as a definite human carcinogen

leptospira_interrogans.transmission: water carrying the urine of infected animals, through broken skin
leptospira_interrogans.makeup: a tightly coiled spirochaete with hooked ends
leptospira_interrogans.durability: weeks in warm fresh water, which is why it follows floods

seriousness.measure: Weil's disease, the severe form

francisella_tularensis.transmission: handling infected hares, tick bites, and contaminated water
francisella_tularensis.makeup: a very small Gram-negative coccobacillus; as few as ten organisms cause disease
francisella_tularensis.durability: weeks in water, mud and carcasses

seriousness.measure: untreated tularaemia

rickettsia_rickettsii.transmission: the bite of an infected tick
rickettsia_rickettsii.reservoir: ticks themselves, which pass it to their own eggs
rickettsia_rickettsii.makeup: an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that cannot make its own ATP
symptoms: a rash that starts at wrists and ankles

seriousness.measure: untreated Rocky Mountain spotted fever

brucella.transmission: unpasteurised milk, and handling birth material from infected animals
brucella.makeup: a small Gram-negative coccobacillus that survives inside macrophages
brucella.durability: months in soil, dust and cheese

seriousness.measure: untreated brucellosis

clostridioides_difficile.transmission: spores on hands and hospital surfaces, after antibiotics have cleared the competition
clostridioides_difficile.reservoir: the human gut, and hospital environments
clostridioides_difficile.makeup: Gram-positive anaerobic spore-former making two large toxins
clostridioides_difficile.durability: spores survive months on surfaces and are unaffected by alcohol gel

seriousness.measure: case fatality within thirty days

pseudomonas_aeruginosa.makeup: Gram-negative rod, 6.3 Mb — a large genome, which is why it can eat almost anything and resist almost everything
pseudomonas_aeruginosa.durability: it grows in distilled water, disinfectant and fuel

seriousness.measure: hospital-acquired bacteraemia

clostridium_perfringens.transmission: wounds contaminated with soil, and food held warm too long
clostridium_perfringens.makeup: a Gram-positive anaerobic rod that ferments tissue and produces gas in it
clostridium_perfringens.durability: spores survive cooking; the classic outbreak is meat cooled slowly

seriousness.measure: gas gangrene, treated

neisseria_gonorrhoeae.makeup: Gram-negative diplococci that take up loose DNA readily, which is how resistance spreads through the species
neisseria_gonorrhoeae.durability: dies within minutes on a dry surface

seriousness.measure: rarely fatal; the harm is infertility and, in newborns, blindness

chlamydia_trachomatis.transmission: sexual contact, and in trachoma by flies and fingers to the eye
chlamydia_trachomatis.makeup: an obligate intracellular bacterium with two forms — one tough and infectious, one that grows only inside a cell
chlamydia_trachomatis.durability: the infectious form survives briefly outside a cell
symptoms: scarred eyelids that turn the lashes inward

seriousness.measure: not fatal; it is the world's leading infectious cause of blindness

actinomyces_israelii.transmission: not transmitted — it is a mouth resident that gets into tissue through injury
actinomyces_israelii.makeup: a Gram-positive branching filamentous anaerobe that looks like a fungus and is not

seriousness.measure: rarely fatal, but it burrows through tissue planes for months

bartonella_henselae.transmission: a cat scratch, the cat having been infected by its fleas
bartonella_henselae.makeup: a small Gram-negative rod that invades red blood cells
bartonella_henselae.durability: survives in flea faeces for days

seriousness.measure: self-limiting in healthy hosts

streptobacillus_moniliformis.transmission: a rat bite, or milk contaminated by rats
streptobacillus_moniliformis.reservoir: rats, in whose nose and throat it lives harmlessly
streptobacillus_moniliformis.makeup: a Gram-negative rod that grows in beaded chains

seriousness.measure: untreated rat-bite fever

plasmodium.transmission: the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito
plasmodium.reservoir: humans, and the mosquito, which is properly the definitive host
plasmodium.makeup: an apicomplexan with a relict chloroplast, the apicoplast, left from a photosynthetic ancestor — and a target because of it
plasmodium.durability: requires a host or a mosquito at every stage

seriousness.measure: untreated falciparum malaria in a non-immune adult

trypanosoma.transmission: the tsetse fly in Africa; the faeces of a kissing bug in the Americas
trypanosoma.reservoir: cattle and wild game in Africa; opossums and armadillos in the Americas
trypanosoma.makeup: a flagellate that changes its entire surface coat faster than antibodies can be made against it
symptoms: and finally sleep reversed and coma

seriousness.measure: untreated African sleeping sickness

leishmania.makeup: a flagellate that lives inside the very macrophages sent to destroy it
symptoms: a slow ulcer at the bite
or fever, wasting and a huge spleen

seriousness.measure: untreated visceral leishmaniasis

entamoeba_histolytica.makeup: an amoeba with no mitochondria, which makes its ATP by fermentation
entamoeba_histolytica.durability: cysts survive weeks in water and are not killed by chlorination at normal doses

seriousness.measure: invasive amoebiasis

naegleria_fowleri.transmission: warm fresh water forced up the nose
naegleria_fowleri.reservoir: warm lakes and poorly chlorinated pools
naegleria_fowleri.makeup: a free-living amoeba that is not a parasite at all and does not benefit from what it does
naegleria_fowleri.durability: thrives up to 45 degrees; it is a heat-loving organism

seriousness.measure: primary amoebic meningoencephalitis

toxoplasma_gondii.transmission: cat faeces, undercooked meat, and across the placenta
toxoplasma_gondii.reservoir: cats, the only host it can complete its sexual cycle in
toxoplasma_gondii.makeup: an apicomplexan that forms lifelong cysts in muscle and brain
toxoplasma_gondii.durability: oocysts survive over a year in moist soil
symptoms: and in the unborn, hydrocephalus and blindness

seriousness.measure: immunocompetent hosts; it kills only where immunity has failed

giardia.makeup: a flagellate with two nuclei and no mitochondria
giardia.durability: cysts survive months in cold water and resist chlorine

seriousness.measure: not fatal, but it can last months and cause lasting lactose intolerance

cryptosporidium.transmission: water — it caused the largest waterborne outbreak on record
cryptosporidium.makeup: an apicomplexan whose oocysts are four micrometres across and pass most water filters
cryptosporidium.durability: oocysts resist chlorine at any dose used in drinking water

seriousness.measure: self-limiting in healthy hosts; in advanced HIV it is a wasting illness that does not stop

balantidium_coli.makeup: the only ciliate that causes human disease, and the largest protozoan that does
balantidium_coli.durability: cysts survive weeks in moist conditions

seriousness.measure: rare and usually mild; it perforates the colon only in the debilitated

trichomonas_vaginalis.makeup: a flagellate with no cyst stage at all, which is why it cannot survive drying
trichomonas_vaginalis.durability: hours at most outside the host

seriousness.measure: not fatal; it raises the risk of acquiring HIV

cyclospora_cayetanensis.transmission: fresh produce washed in contaminated water
cyclospora_cayetanensis.makeup: an apicomplexan whose oocysts need days outside a host to become infectious — so it never passes directly person to person
cyclospora_cayetanensis.durability: oocysts need one to two weeks to mature, then persist

seriousness.measure: not fatal in healthy hosts

pneumocystis_jirovecii.transmission: air, and almost everyone is exposed in childhood
pneumocystis_jirovecii.makeup: a fungus with no ergosterol in its membrane, which is why the usual antifungals do nothing to it

seriousness.measure: untreated pneumocystis pneumonia in advanced HIV

dermatophyte.transmission: skin contact, floors, and shared towels
dermatophyte.reservoir: humans, animals and soil, depending on species
dermatophyte.makeup: moulds that digest keratin and grow only in dead skin, hair and nail
dermatophyte.durability: spores survive months on floors and in shoes

seriousness.measure: never fatal; the point is that it is the commonest fungal infection there is

prion.transmission: eating infected nervous tissue, and surgical instruments
prion.reservoir: cattle for BSE; sheep for scrapie; and it arises spontaneously too
prion.makeup: no genome at all — a normal host protein refolded, which then converts its neighbours
prion.durability: survives autoclaving, formalin and years in soil; standard sterilisation does not touch it

seriousness.measure: invariably fatal; there has never been a survivor of any prion disease

phytophthora_infestans.transmission: wind-blown sporangia, and infected seed tubers
phytophthora_infestans.reservoir: potato and tomato; it overwinters in tubers left in the ground
phytophthora_infestans.makeup: an oomycete with cellulose walls and diploid nuclei — nothing like a fungus; 240 Mb, an unusually large genome padded with repeats that let its attack genes evolve fast
phytophthora_infestans.durability: sporangia last hours in sunlight and days in cool damp; the mycelium overwinters in a tuber
symptoms: blackened leaf patches with a pale halo

seriousness.measure: an untreated susceptible crop in a wet season is a total loss, which is what happened in Ireland from 1845

puccinia_graminis.reservoir: wheat, and barberry for the sexual stage
puccinia_graminis.makeup: a basidiomycete with five spore stages across two unrelated hosts
puccinia_graminis.durability: urediniospores survive days to weeks in the air; the overwintering stage needs barberry or a green bridge
symptoms: red-brown pustules bursting through the stem

seriousness.measure: yield loss in a susceptible variety under a severe epidemic

hemileia_vastatrix.makeup: a basidiomycete whose spores are borne on the leaf underside and germinate only through the stomata there
hemileia_vastatrix.durability: spores survive about six weeks off the plant

seriousness.measure: yield loss in an unsprayed susceptible plantation; Ceylon's industry fell from third in the world to nothing in twenty years

magnaporthe_oryzae.makeup: an ascomycete that builds an appressorium and raises its internal pressure to about 8 MPa to punch through the intact leaf
magnaporthe_oryzae.durability: conidia survive weeks; the fungus overwinters in straw and seed

seriousness.measure: yield loss in a severe epidemic; global losses are enough rice for tens of millions of people a year

fusarium_oxysporum.transmission: soil, water, and machinery carrying infected earth
fusarium_oxysporum.makeup: an ascomycete whose chlamydospores are thick-walled resting cells
fusarium_oxysporum.durability: chlamydospores stay viable in soil for thirty years and more

seriousness.measure: an infected plant does not recover, and an infected field cannot grow the crop again within a working lifetime

botrytis_cinerea.transmission: airborne conidia landing on damaged or senescing tissue
botrytis_cinerea.reservoir: almost any soft plant tissue; over 200 hosts
botrytis_cinerea.makeup: an ascomycete that kills tissue ahead of itself with oxalic acid and reactive oxygen, then eats what it killed
botrytis_cinerea.durability: sclerotia overwinter in debris; conidia are everywhere in the air
symptoms: in dry conditions instead, shrivelled concentrated grapes

seriousness.measure: post-harvest and field loss in soft fruit; the same organism is deliberately encouraged for Sauternes

erysiphe.transmission: wind, and it does not need the leaf to be wet
erysiphe.reservoir: a very wide host range, each species narrow
erysiphe.makeup: an ascomycete that stays on the leaf surface and feeds through haustoria pushed into the epidermal cells only
erysiphe.durability: chasmothecia overwinter in debris and on buds
symptoms: white powder on the upper leaf

seriousness.measure: yield loss; it disfigures far more often than it kills

plasmopara_viticola.transmission: rain splash and free water on the leaf
plasmopara_viticola.reservoir: grapevine; it overwinters as oospores in fallen leaves
plasmopara_viticola.makeup: an oomycete releasing motile zoospores that swim to the stomata
plasmopara_viticola.durability: oospores survive winter in leaf litter and several years in soil

seriousness.measure: crop loss in a wet season without treatment; it nearly ended European viticulture in the 1880s

claviceps_purpurea.transmission: wind-blown spores infecting the open flower, and insects drawn to the honeydew
claviceps_purpurea.reservoir: rye above all, and other grasses
claviceps_purpurea.makeup: an ascomycete that replaces the ovary with a sclerotium loaded with ergoline alkaloids
claviceps_purpurea.durability: sclerotia survive a year in soil and remain toxic in stored grain
symptoms: a hard black spur where the grain should be

seriousness.measure: case fatality in historical ergotism outbreaks; the 944 AD outbreak in France is said to have killed some 40,000 people

ustilago_maydis.transmission: wind-blown teliospores entering through wounds and silks
ustilago_maydis.makeup: a basidiomycete that is a harmless yeast until two compatible cells fuse — only the fused form can infect
ustilago_maydis.durability: teliospores stay viable in soil and manure for years
symptoms: grey galls on cob, tassel or stem, bursting into black spores

seriousness.measure: yield loss where it is a disease; in Mexico the gall sells for more than the maize

venturia_inaequalis.transmission: ascospores fired upward from fallen leaves in spring rain
venturia_inaequalis.makeup: an ascomycete that grows between the cuticle and the epidermis rather than inside the cells
venturia_inaequalis.durability: overwinters entirely in dead leaves on the ground

seriousness.measure: loss of marketable fruit in an unmanaged susceptible orchard

ophiostoma_ulmi.transmission: elm bark beetles feeding in twig crotches, and root grafts between neighbouring trees
ophiostoma_ulmi.reservoir: dead and dying elms, where the beetles breed
ophiostoma_ulmi.makeup: an ascomycete that grows as yeast-like spores carried in the sap stream
ophiostoma_ulmi.durability: survives in dead bark as long as the beetles breed there
symptoms: yellowing and wilting on one branch first
death in one or two seasons

seriousness.measure: mortality of mature susceptible elms; Britain lost about 25 million trees

cryphonectria_parasitica.transmission: wind and rain-splashed spores entering through bark wounds
cryphonectria_parasitica.reservoir: oaks and Asian chestnuts, which tolerate it
cryphonectria_parasitica.makeup: an ascomycete that can itself be infected by a virus, and a virus-infected strain is much less aggressive

seriousness.measure: mortality of the aboveground American chestnut; about four billion trees

hymenoscyphus_fraxineus.transmission: wind-blown ascospores from fruiting bodies on last year's leaf stalks
hymenoscyphus_fraxineus.reservoir: the leaf litter under the trees
hymenoscyphus_fraxineus.makeup: an ascomycete native to east Asia, where it is a harmless leaf endophyte of Manchurian ash
hymenoscyphus_fraxineus.durability: fruits on the previous year's leaf stalks in the litter
symptoms: black lesions at leaf and twig junctions

seriousness.measure: mortality of European ash; a small proportion show heritable tolerance, which is the only hope for the species

xylella_fastidiosa.reservoir: a very wide range of plants, many symptomless
xylella_fastidiosa.makeup: a Gram-negative bacterium restricted to the xylem, with a small 2.7 Mb genome and no flagella
xylella_fastidiosa.durability: survives only inside a host or its insect vector

seriousness.measure: mortality of infected olive trees in the Puglia outbreak, some of them centuries old

candidatus_liberibacter.makeup: a phloem-limited bacterium that has never been grown in culture — which is what Candidatus means
candidatus_liberibacter.durability: cannot survive outside a host or vector
symptoms: lopsided fruit that stays green at the base

seriousness.measure: an infected tree does not recover; Florida's orange production has fallen about 90% since it arrived

erwinia_amylovora.transmission: bees and rain moving bacteria into open flowers
erwinia_amylovora.reservoir: cankers on the tree, which ooze in spring
erwinia_amylovora.makeup: a Gram-negative rod producing amylovoran, an exopolysaccharide that blocks the vessels
erwinia_amylovora.durability: overwinters in bark cankers; ooze is infectious for days
symptoms: blackened shoots hooked at the tip

seriousness.measure: loss of infected apple and pear trees in a severe outbreak; the first plant disease proved to be bacterial, in 1878

agrobacterium_tumefaciens.transmission: soil entering wounds, especially at grafting and transplanting
agrobacterium_tumefaciens.makeup: a Gram-negative rod carrying a tumour-inducing plasmid whose T-DNA integrates into the plant's own chromosomes
agrobacterium_tumefaciens.durability: survives in soil and in galls for years
symptoms: a rough tumour at the crown
rarely, death of a young plant

seriousness.measure: loss in nursery stock; its importance is not as a disease but as the standard means of putting genes into plants

plasmodiophora_brassicae.transmission: soil, water and boots; motile zoospores swim to the root hairs
plasmodiophora_brassicae.reservoir: the soil, for up to twenty years
plasmodiophora_brassicae.makeup: not a fungus but a protist — a plasmodium with no cell wall living inside the root cells
plasmodiophora_brassicae.durability: resting spores stay viable in soil for up to twenty years
symptoms: wilting in sun despite wet soil

seriousness.measure: yield loss in infested land; the spore longevity puts it outside any normal rotation

rhizoctonia_solani.makeup: a basidiomycete that usually never makes spores at all and spreads entirely as mycelium
rhizoctonia_solani.durability: sclerotia and mycelium persist in soil for years
symptoms: seedlings pinched through at soil level
bare patches in a seed tray

seriousness.measure: seedling loss in an infested seedbed

verticillium_dahliae.makeup: an ascomycete forming microsclerotia — tiny black resting bodies rather than spores
verticillium_dahliae.durability: microsclerotia survive in soil for ten to fifteen years
symptoms: wilting in the afternoon and recovering overnight

seriousness.measure: yield loss; it is chronic rather than sudden and rarely kills outright

pseudomonas_syringae.reservoir: leaf surfaces almost everywhere, and clouds
pseudomonas_syringae.makeup: a Gram-negative rod carrying an ice-nucleation protein that templates a crystal at about minus two degrees
pseudomonas_syringae.durability: survives on leaf surfaces, in water and in the atmosphere

seriousness.measure: yield loss across many crops; the same protein it damages plants with is what snow machines use

potato_virus_y.transmission: aphids, on the mouthparts, in seconds of probing
potato_virus_y.makeup: single positive-strand RNA potyvirus, about 9.7 kb, in a flexuous rod
potato_virus_y.durability: survives only in living plant tissue and tubers

seriousness.measure: yield loss in a susceptible variety; insecticide barely helps because the aphid transmits before it dies

barley_yellow_dwarf_virus.transmission: aphids only, and only by feeding deeply enough to reach the phloem
barley_yellow_dwarf_virus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA luteovirus confined to the phloem; it cannot be transmitted by sap or contact
barley_yellow_dwarf_virus.durability: persists in the aphid for the insect's life, and in living plants

seriousness.measure: yield loss; it is the most widespread viral disease of cereals in the world

foot_and_mouth_virus.transmission: breath, saliva, milk, and on boots and vehicles
foot_and_mouth_virus.reservoir: cloven-hoofed animals; carriers persist in cattle for months
foot_and_mouth_virus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA picornavirus, 8.5 kb, bare capsid, with seven serotypes that give no cross-immunity
foot_and_mouth_virus.durability: a month on straw and in soil in cool damp weather; it survives in bone marrow and lymph nodes of chilled carcasses
symptoms: blisters on tongue, feet and teats

seriousness.measure: mortality in adult cattle, which is low — the 2001 British cull of over six million animals was a trade measure, not a medical one

rinderpest_virus.reservoir: cattle and buffalo only, which is why eradication was possible
rinderpest_virus.makeup: single negative-strand RNA morbillivirus, closest relative of measles
rinderpest_virus.durability: poor survival outside the host — it needs a continuous chain of animals

seriousness.measure: mortality in naive cattle; its 1890s arrival in Africa killed about 90% of the cattle in the east

african_swine_fever_virus.transmission: direct contact, ticks, and pork products carried by people
african_swine_fever_virus.reservoir: warthogs and soft ticks, in which it is harmless
african_swine_fever_virus.makeup: a very large double-stranded DNA virus, 170-190 kb, and the only member of its own family — which is much of why no vaccine has worked
african_swine_fever_virus.durability: months in frozen and cured pork, and weeks in blood at room temperature

seriousness.measure: mortality in domestic pigs from the virulent genotypes

avian_influenza.transmission: faeces and water in wild birds; air and dust in poultry houses
avian_influenza.reservoir: wild waterfowl, in which it is a symptomless gut infection
avian_influenza.makeup: eight segments of negative-strand RNA; the segments are what let two strains reassort into something new
avian_influenza.durability: weeks in cold water — which is how it persists between migrations
symptoms: in poultry, sudden death and swollen heads

seriousness.measure: mortality in poultry from highly pathogenic strains; H5N1 in humans is around 0.5 but has never transmitted person to person

newcastle_disease_virus.makeup: single negative-strand RNA paramyxovirus; its virulence turns on a single cleavage site in the fusion protein
newcastle_disease_virus.durability: weeks in faeces and on eggshells

seriousness.measure: mortality in unvaccinated poultry from velogenic strains

bluetongue_virus.transmission: the bite of a Culicoides midge, and nothing else
bluetongue_virus.reservoir: cattle, which show little sign of it, and wild ruminants
bluetongue_virus.makeup: ten segments of double-stranded RNA in a bare capsid
bluetongue_virus.durability: requires the midge; it does not persist in the environment
symptoms: a blue tongue in the worst cases

seriousness.measure: mortality in naive sheep; cattle carry it almost without signs

canine_parvovirus.transmission: faeces, and it is on every surface a dog has walked over
canine_parvovirus.reservoir: dogs, and the environment, for a long time
canine_parvovirus.makeup: single-stranded DNA, only 5 kb — one of the smallest viruses there is, and it needs a dividing cell to copy itself
canine_parvovirus.durability: over a year in soil, and it resists most household disinfectants

seriousness.measure: mortality in untreated puppies; with fluids and care it falls below 0.1

myxoma_virus.transmission: mosquitoes and fleas, mechanically on the mouthparts
myxoma_virus.reservoir: South American cottontails, in which it causes a harmless skin lump
myxoma_virus.durability: survives in the vector and in dried material for weeks

seriousness.measure: mortality of European rabbits in the first Australian year; within a decade the virus had become milder and the rabbits more resistant, and it settled far short of extermination

batrachochytrium.transmission: water, and on the boots and equipment of people moving between ponds
batrachochytrium.reservoir: amphibians, and some tolerant carrier species
batrachochytrium.makeup: a chytrid — a fungus with a swimming, flagellated spore, which almost no other fungus has
batrachochytrium.durability: zoospores survive weeks in water and on damp equipment
symptoms: death from cardiac arrest brought on by lost electrolytes

seriousness.measure: mortality in susceptible species during an outbreak; implicated in the decline of about 500 amphibian species and the extinction of roughly 90 — more than any other single pathogen on record

white_nose_fungus.transmission: bat to bat, and on caving gear
white_nose_fungus.reservoir: European bats, which tolerate it, and cave sediment
white_nose_fungus.makeup: a cold-loving ascomycete that grows between 4 and 15 degrees and dies above 20
white_nose_fungus.durability: persists in cave sediment between winters
symptoms: white fuzz on muzzle and wings

seriousness.measure: mortality in affected North American hibernacula; some species have declined over 90% since 2006

varroa_mite.transmission: bee to bee, and between colonies on drifting and robbing bees
varroa_mite.reservoir: the Asian honey bee, which grooms it off and seals infested brood
varroa_mite.makeup: an eight-legged mite that feeds on the bee's fat body — not, as long thought, on its blood
varroa_mite.durability: cannot live long off a bee; it reproduces only in sealed brood
symptoms: and the collapse of the colony over a season or two

seriousness.measure: colony loss within two to three years if untreated; most losses blamed on other causes trace back to this mite and the viruses it delivers

paenibacillus_larvae.transmission: spores in honey and on comb, fed to larvae by nurse bees
paenibacillus_larvae.makeup: a Gram-positive spore-forming rod; a single spore is enough to kill a young larva
paenibacillus_larvae.durability: spores stay viable in comb and equipment for over fifty years and survive anything short of fire
symptoms: a ropy brown mass in the cell

seriousness.measure: an infected colony does not recover; burning the bees and the boxes is still the standard answer in most of the world

nosema.transmission: spores in faeces, picked up while cleaning the comb
nosema.makeup: a microsporidian — a fungus that has discarded its own mitochondria and takes finished ATP from the host cell
nosema.durability: spores survive a year in comb and resist drying
symptoms: a colony that dwindles without obvious cause

seriousness.measure: colony loss where it is heavy; more often it shortens lives and reduces the crop without killing outright

dirofilaria_immitis.transmission: mosquitoes; the larvae must spend about two weeks in one and cannot develop otherwise
dirofilaria_immitis.makeup: a nematode up to 30 cm long, living in the pulmonary artery and right heart
dirofilaria_immitis.durability: cannot survive outside a host or vector

seriousness.measure: mortality in untreated advanced infection; killing the adult worms too fast is itself dangerous, because the dead worms lodge in the lung

sarcoptes_scabiei.reservoir: humans and many mammals, as host-adapted strains of one species
sarcoptes_scabiei.makeup: a mite about 0.3 mm across that tunnels in the outer skin and lays eggs behind it
sarcoptes_scabiei.durability: two to three days off a host
symptoms: in animals, hair loss and crusting

seriousness.measure: rarely fatal in itself; crusted scabies in the immunosuppressed is dangerous through secondary infection

theileria.transmission: the bite of an infected tick
theileria.makeup: an apicomplexan that infects white blood cells and makes them divide like a cancer, dividing with them so every daughter cell is infected

seriousness.measure: mortality in naive cattle from East Coast fever; it is the only eukaryotic parasite known to transform a host cell this way, and killing it lets the cells behave normally again

babesia.transmission: the bite of an infected tick
babesia.makeup: an apicomplexan that lives inside red blood cells and bursts them
babesia.durability: requires the tick, which passes it to its own eggs
symptoms: red urine from broken red cells

seriousness.measure: mortality in naive cattle with Texas cattle fever; proving a tick carried it in 1893 was the first demonstration that any arthropod transmits any disease

vibrio_cholerae.transmission: water and food contaminated with faeces
vibrio_cholerae.reservoir: brackish water and plankton, where it lives quite happily without people
vibrio_cholerae.makeup: a comma-shaped Gram-negative rod with a single polar flagellum; the toxin gene is carried by a bacteriophage
vibrio_cholerae.durability: weeks in water, and it attaches to the chitin of copepods

seriousness.measure: untreated severe cholera; with rehydration alone it falls below 0.01, which is one of the largest gaps between treated and untreated in all of medicine

ascaris_lumbricoides.transmission: eggs swallowed from soil contaminated with human faeces
ascaris_lumbricoides.reservoir: humans and the soil around them
ascaris_lumbricoides.makeup: a nematode up to 35 cm long; a female lays around 200,000 eggs a day
ascaris_lumbricoides.durability: eggs stay infective in soil for up to ten years and resist most disinfectants
symptoms: a cough as the larvae cross the lung
obstruction where the worms are many

seriousness.measure: case fatality, almost all from bowel obstruction in children; it infects on the order of 800 million people

enterobius_vermicularis.transmission: eggs on fingers, bedding and dust — swallowed, not entered through skin
enterobius_vermicularis.makeup: a small nematode, the female about a centimetre, which crawls out at night to lay on the skin
enterobius_vermicularis.durability: eggs survive two to three weeks on surfaces and become infective in hours

seriousness.measure: never fatal; it is simply the commonest worm infection in temperate countries

taenia_solium.transmission: undercooked pork for the tapeworm; swallowed eggs for the dangerous form
taenia_solium.makeup: a tapeworm several metres long with a head of hooks and suckers, and no gut of its own
taenia_solium.durability: eggs survive months in the environment
symptoms: often nothing from the worm itself
seizures where the larvae lodge in the brain

seriousness.measure: case fatality of untreated neurocysticercosis; it is the single commonest preventable cause of epilepsy worldwide

echinococcus_granulosus.reservoir: dogs, with sheep as the intermediate host
echinococcus_granulosus.makeup: a tapeworm only a few millimetres long in the dog; in the wrong host it forms a fluid-filled cyst instead
echinococcus_granulosus.durability: eggs survive a year in cool damp conditions
symptoms: a slowly growing cyst in liver or lung
and shock if the cyst bursts

seriousness.measure: case fatality with treatment; over 0.5 if a cyst is left and ruptures

trichinella_spiralis.makeup: a nematode whose larvae coil inside a muscle cell they have reprogrammed into a nurse cell that feeds them
trichinella_spiralis.durability: larvae survive in muscle for years, and in a frozen carcass for weeks
symptoms: then fever, muscle pain and swelling around the eyes

seriousness.measure: case fatality; the heavy infections that killed were a feature of the era before meat inspection

wuchereria_bancrofti.reservoir: humans only, which is why elimination is possible
wuchereria_bancrofti.makeup: a filarial nematode living in the lymphatic vessels; its microfilariae circulate at night, timed to the mosquito
symptoms: and in time the gross thickening called elephantiasis

seriousness.measure: not fatal; it is one of the leading causes of permanent disability in the world

onchocerca_volvulus.transmission: blackflies breeding in fast rivers, which is why it is called river blindness
onchocerca_volvulus.makeup: a filarial nematode carrying Wolbachia bacteria inside it, without which it cannot reproduce
symptoms: and blindness from the inflammation around dying larvae

seriousness.measure: not fatal; it blinded whole riverside villages before ivermectin, and the drug is donated free for it

strongyloides_stercoralis.transmission: larvae entering through the skin from contaminated soil
strongyloides_stercoralis.reservoir: humans, and it can complete its whole cycle inside one
strongyloides_stercoralis.makeup: a nematode that reproduces inside the host, so an infection acquired once can persist for a lifetime
strongyloides_stercoralis.durability: free-living generations survive in warm moist soil
symptoms: and in the immunosuppressed, overwhelming spread

seriousness.measure: case fatality of hyperinfection, which is what happens when someone carrying it silently is given steroids

dracunculus_medinensis.transmission: drinking water containing the copepods that carry its larvae
dracunculus_medinensis.makeup: a nematode up to a metre long, which emerges slowly through a blister in the skin
dracunculus_medinensis.durability: larvae survive weeks in water inside a copepod
symptoms: a burning blister, usually on the leg
and a worm that takes weeks to come out

seriousness.measure: never fatal; it is on the edge of eradication, from 3.5 million cases in 1986 to a handful a year, achieved with cloth filters and behaviour change and no drug or vaccine at all

epstein_barr_virus.reservoir: humans; over 90% of adults carry it for life
epstein_barr_virus.makeup: double-stranded DNA herpesvirus, 172 kb, which settles permanently in B cells
epstein_barr_virus.durability: latent in the host's own cells for life
symptoms: fever, sore throat and exhaustion if caught later

seriousness.measure: the acute illness is rarely fatal; the weight of it is Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and the strongest known trigger for multiple sclerosis

eimeria.transmission: oocysts in litter and faeces, swallowed while feeding
eimeria.reservoir: poultry and livestock, and the ground they stand on
eimeria.makeup: an apicomplexan, each species locked to one host and usually one part of one gut
eimeria.durability: oocysts survive months in litter and resist most disinfectants

seriousness.measure: mortality in an untreated outbreak in young poultry; it is reckoned the most economically damaging disease in the poultry industry

variola.reservoir: humans only — and that is why it could be eradicated
variola.makeup: double-stranded DNA poxvirus, about 186 kb, brick-shaped
variola.durability: very durable; it survives years in dried scab material
symptoms: a rash whose lesions all advance together

seriousness.measure: variola major in the unvaccinated; declared eradicated in 1980, the only human disease ever ended

sars_cov_2.reservoir: bats, with an intermediate host still argued over
sars_cov_2.makeup: single positive-strand RNA, about 30 kb — the largest genome of any RNA virus, held together by a proofreading enzyme
sars_cov_2.durability: hours in air as fine aerosol; days on some surfaces, though surface spread proved minor

seriousness.measure: infection fatality rate before vaccines, rising steeply with age; it spreads before symptoms, which is why the SARS containment strategy failed on it

coronavirus.reservoir: bats above all, and many mammals
coronavirus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA with a crown of spike proteins; the only RNA viruses with proofreading
coronavirus.durability: hours to days depending on the strain and surface

seriousness.measure: most coronaviruses cause common colds; the family's importance is that three of them have crossed into humans and been lethal

ebola_virus.transmission: contact with blood and body fluids of the very ill or the newly dead
ebola_virus.makeup: single negative-strand RNA filovirus, a long filament about 19 kb
ebola_virus.durability: days in body fluids; it is not airborne

seriousness.measure: average case fatality across outbreaks, ranging 0.25 to 0.9; it is stopped by contact tracing and burial practice rather than by medicine

marburg_virus.transmission: contact with body fluids, and with infected bats in mines
marburg_virus.makeup: a filovirus, the first ever identified — in Marburg in 1967, from imported monkey tissue

seriousness.measure: average case fatality across outbreaks

lassa_virus.transmission: dust and food contaminated with the urine of the multimammate rat
lassa_virus.reservoir: one species of rat that lives inside houses across West Africa
lassa_virus.makeup: an arenavirus with two RNA segments, which picks up host ribosomes into its own particle

seriousness.measure: case fatality overall, about 0.15 among those admitted to hospital; the commonest lasting harm is deafness, not death

nipah_virus.transmission: pigs in the first outbreak; raw date palm sap in the later ones
nipah_virus.durability: days in date palm sap; it is inactivated by heat

seriousness.measure: case fatality in the Bangladesh outbreaks

hantavirus.transmission: breathing dust from dried rodent urine and droppings — almost never person to person
hantavirus.reservoir: rodents, each virus with its own species
hantavirus.makeup: a bunyavirus with three RNA segments
hantavirus.durability: survives in dried excreta for days
symptoms: then either kidney failure or sudden lung oedema

seriousness.measure: case fatality of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the Americas; the Eurasian kidney form is under 0.01

dengue_virus.transmission: Aedes aegypti, a mosquito that bites by day and lives in cities
dengue_virus.reservoir: humans and mosquitoes, in an urban cycle needing no animal at all
dengue_virus.makeup: single positive-strand RNA flavivirus, four serotypes that do not cross-protect
symptoms: and in the severe form, plasma leak

seriousness.measure: severe dengue with care, and around 0.2 without; severe cases are usually a SECOND infection, because antibody to one serotype helps another into the cell

zika_virus.transmission: Aedes mosquitoes, sex, and across the placenta
symptoms: mild fever and rash, or nothing
and in the unborn, a small brain

seriousness.measure: the infection itself is trivial; the harm is congenital, and it took an epidemic in a large non-immune population before an effect that rare became visible at all

chikungunya_virus.reservoir: humans, and primates in a forest cycle
symptoms: joint pain severe enough to bend the sufferer up
and arthritis lasting months or years

seriousness.measure: case fatality; the burden is chronic arthritis rather than death, and one envelope mutation in 2005 gave it the tiger mosquito and most of the tropics

hepatitis_b.transmission: blood, sex, and mother to child at birth
hepatitis_b.reservoir: humans; around 250 million carry it chronically
hepatitis_b.makeup: a partly double-stranded DNA virus that copies itself through an RNA intermediate, as a retrovirus does
hepatitis_b.durability: at least a week in dried blood, and it is roughly a hundred times more infectious than HIV by the same exposure

seriousness.measure: lifetime risk of death from cirrhosis or liver cancer among chronic carriers; whether it becomes chronic depends almost entirely on the age at infection

hepatitis_c.transmission: blood, overwhelmingly through shared needles and unscreened transfusion
hepatitis_c.makeup: single positive-strand RNA flavivirus that mutates fast enough to stay ahead of antibody
hepatitis_c.durability: up to three weeks on surfaces in dried blood

seriousness.measure: lifetime risk of cirrhosis in untreated chronic infection — but direct-acting antivirals now cure over 95% in weeks, so this is one of the few chronic viral infections that can simply be ended

herpes_simplex.transmission: direct contact with skin or mucosa, often from someone with no symptoms
herpes_simplex.reservoir: humans; most of the world carries HSV-1
herpes_simplex.makeup: double-stranded DNA herpesvirus, 152 kb, which hides in the cell bodies of sensory nerves
herpes_simplex.durability: latent for life in a place the immune system does not police, because killing neurons is worse than tolerating passengers
symptoms: cold sores or genital ulcers, recurring in the same place

seriousness.measure: trivial in a healthy adult; neonatal herpes, caught at birth, has an untreated case fatality around 0.6

varicella_zoster.transmission: air, and contact with the fluid in the blisters
varicella_zoster.makeup: double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that retreats to the dorsal root ganglia
varicella_zoster.durability: latent for life; the airborne form survives only briefly

seriousness.measure: case fatality of chickenpox in healthy children; shingles is rarely fatal but the nerve pain after it can last years

rotavirus.transmission: faecal-oral, and hygiene barely reduces it
rotavirus.reservoir: humans, and it infects essentially every child by five
rotavirus.makeup: eleven segments of double-stranded RNA in a triple-layered bare capsid

seriousness.measure: case fatality where rehydration is unavailable; before the vaccine it killed around half a million children a year, and the same proportion caught it in countries with clean water as without

mycobacterium_leprae.transmission: prolonged close contact, and most people exposed never develop it
mycobacterium_leprae.makeup: a mycobacterium that has lost about a third of its genes to decay and cannot be grown in any culture medium
mycobacterium_leprae.durability: divides once every fortnight — the slowest of any known bacterium, which is why the disease takes years to appear
symptoms: and injury to numb hands and feet

seriousness.measure: not fatal; the disability comes from unnoticed injury to anaesthetic limbs, and it is curable with multidrug therapy

borrelia_burgdorferi.transmission: the bite of an Ixodes tick, usually attached over a day
borrelia_burgdorferi.reservoir: mice and deer, with the tick as the link
borrelia_burgdorferi.makeup: a spirochaete whose genome is split across a chromosome and over twenty plasmids — no other bacterium is organised like that
borrelia_burgdorferi.durability: cannot survive outside a host or tick
symptoms: and later, nerve and heart involvement

seriousness.measure: rarely fatal; untreated it becomes a chronic arthritis and neuropathy, and it swaps its surface coat between tick and mammal

shigella.transmission: person to person, food and water — and ten organisms are enough
shigella.makeup: genetically Escherichia coli, kept as a separate genus for historical reasons; it invades the colon lining rather than sitting on it
shigella.durability: days on hands and surfaces; weeks in water

seriousness.measure: case fatality with treatment, up to 0.15 in epidemics of S. dysenteriae without it

candida_albicans.transmission: not really transmitted — most people already carry it
candida_albicans.reservoir: the human mouth, gut and skin
candida_albicans.makeup: a yeast that switches to a filamentous hyphal form to penetrate tissue, triggered by body temperature, neutral pH and serum
candida_albicans.durability: survives on skin and surfaces for days

seriousness.measure: case fatality of invasive candidaemia; it is the clearest case of an organism that is a pathogen only in relation to a host whose defences are down

aspergillus_fumigatus.transmission: breathing in spores, of which everyone inhales hundreds a day
aspergillus_fumigatus.reservoir: compost, dust and decaying vegetation everywhere
aspergillus_fumigatus.makeup: a mould whose spores are 2 to 3 micrometres — exactly the size that reaches the deepest airway
aspergillus_fumigatus.durability: spores survive indefinitely in dust and compost
symptoms: nothing at all in a healthy person
and in the immunosuppressed, an invasive pneumonia

seriousness.measure: case fatality of invasive aspergillosis; almost nobody with working lungs is harmed by it at all

cryptococcus_neoformans.transmission: breathing in spores from pigeon droppings and tree hollows
cryptococcus_neoformans.reservoir: birds, which carry it without being infected
cryptococcus_neoformans.makeup: a yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule too slippery for a white cell to grip
cryptococcus_neoformans.durability: survives for years in dried pigeon droppings

seriousness.measure: case fatality of cryptococcal meningitis in low-resource settings; it remains one of the commonest causes of death in advanced HIV

schistosoma_mansoni.transmission: larvae penetrating skin in fresh water
schistosoma_mansoni.reservoir: humans, and freshwater snails as the intermediate host
schistosoma_mansoni.makeup: a fluke whose male and female live permanently paired, the female held in a groove along the male's body
schistosoma_mansoni.durability: cercariae survive about 48 hours in water
symptoms: and years later, liver fibrosis from eggs lodged in tissue

seriousness.measure: case fatality; the damage is done by the eggs rather than the worms, and irrigation and dams spread it by spreading the snail

necator_americanus.transmission: larvae penetrating the skin of a bare foot from contaminated soil
necator_americanus.reservoir: humans and the soil around them
necator_americanus.makeup: a nematode about a centimetre long that cuts into the gut wall and feeds on the blood
necator_americanus.durability: larvae survive weeks in warm moist shaded soil
symptoms: an itchy rash at the entry point
cough as they cross the lung

seriousness.measure: rarely fatal; the harm is chronic iron loss, and in children a lasting deficit in growth and schooling

canine_distemper_virus.transmission: air and shared bowls, between dogs and out into wild carnivores
canine_distemper_virus.reservoir: domestic dogs, and wild carnivores once it is out
canine_distemper_virus.makeup: single negative-strand RNA morbillivirus — a close relative of measles and rinderpest
canine_distemper_virus.durability: poor survival outside a host; it needs a continuous chain

seriousness.measure: mortality in unvaccinated dogs; it killed about a third of the Serengeti lions in 1994, having come from village dogs, so vaccinating dogs is a wildlife measure

feline_leukaemia_virus.transmission: saliva — grooming, shared bowls and bites
feline_leukaemia_virus.makeup: a retrovirus that writes a DNA copy of itself into the cat's own chromosomes
feline_leukaemia_virus.durability: minutes outside the host; it is fragile

seriousness.measure: three-year mortality in persistently infected cats; most of the harm is where the virus inserts itself rather than anything it makes, and that mechanism is how the first oncogenes were found
